# Abstract

This paper will examine whether everyday adaptive functioning and autonomy,
measured with ABAS-II, and everyday executive functioning, measured with
BRIEF-2, are associated with children's baseline navigational and visuospatial
abilities. The analysis is cross-sectional and uses only PRE scores from the
final database, treating the sample as if no training and no second assessment
had occurred.

# Introduction

Children's ability to navigate space develops within everyday relationships,
opportunities for movement, and repeated interactions with meaningful
environments. A broad developmental perspective suggests that attachment
relationships, autonomy-supportive contexts, and embodied motor experience may
all contribute to how children explore, plan routes, remember spatial
locations, and solve navigation-like problems.

In this preliminary version, the theoretical background is intentionally brief.
The final introduction will expand the links among attachment theory, autonomy,
motor experience, adaptive functioning, executive functioning, and navigational
development.

# Methods

## Participants

The analytic sample includes all valid participants from the final database
used in the larger project. The present paper does not use training group,
POST scores, or PRE-to-POST change. All analyses are based on baseline/PRE
measures only.

## Measures

Children completed baseline cognitive, visuospatial, and Minefield measures.
Teacher questionnaires included ABAS-II adaptive functioning scales and BRIEF-2
everyday executive-function scales and indices. ABAS and BRIEF total scores
were derived in the analysis pipeline.

### Minefield Variables

The Minefield task includes working-memory, planning, and working-memory plus
planning conditions. PRE outcome variables include accuracy, span/trial
measures, route-efficiency percentages, time measures, error/obstacle-related
measures, and derived composite scores. Time variables are also available as
log-transformed PRE scores when defined by the shared project pipeline.

## Statistical Analysis

The analysis was run with:

```powershell
python abas_brief_navigation_paper\analysis\run_analysis.py
```

Descriptive analyses summarized sample composition, missingness, questionnaire
scores, and PRE outcomes. Questionnaire-PRE associations were tested with both
Pearson and Spearman correlations. Primary regression models predicted each
standardized PRE outcome from each standardized ABAS/BRIEF variable, adjusting
for standardized age:

```text
outcome_PRE_z ~ questionnaire_z + age_z
```

HC3 robust standard errors were used. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction was
applied within each result family. The main text reports FDR-significant
results only. Additional sensitivity outputs include Minefield-only focus
models and models additionally adjusting for Raven PRE accuracy.

The dedicated total-and-subscale analysis excluded Raven from the outcome
set. Its primary sample excluded the two children flagged by the age-specific
Raven screening cut-offs (n = 99), and the full sample (n = 101) was analysed
as a sensitivity check. Twenty-five curated PRE outcomes were tested in
separate blocks for complete-case ABAS and BRIEF totals, eight standard ABAS
scales, nine standard BRIEF scales, and the BRIEF BRI, ERI, and CRI indices.
ABAS supplemental `suppongo` variables were excluded. Each standardized model
was estimated with HC3 robust standard errors first adjusting for age and then
adjusting for age plus Raven PRE accuracy, using identical complete cases for
the paired specifications. FDR correction was applied separately within each
prespecified predictor block.

# Discussion

The discussion will interpret whether teacher-rated autonomy, adaptive
functioning, and everyday executive functioning are associated with baseline
navigational and visuospatial skills. It will also distinguish associations
that appear specific to Minefield navigation outcomes from broader associations
with Raven, Corsi, and Tower of London performance.

Limitations to expand include the cross-sectional design, multiple testing,
teacher-report measurement, missingness in supplemental ABAS variables, and the
need to separate adaptive autonomy from general cognitive development.
